name: application/geo+json
description:
GeoJSON encodes geographic features as JSON, defined by RFC 7946. A document is a Feature or a FeatureCollection, and each feature pairs a geometry (Point, LineString, Polygon, or their multi- forms) with arbitrary properties.

RFC 7946 pinned the coordinate reference system to WGS 84 with longitude before latitude. That single decision removed the largest source of disagreement between implementations of the earlier community specification.

name: application/json-patch+json
description:
JSON Patch describes a change to a JSON document, defined by RFC 6902. A patch is an array of operations, each naming one of add, remove, replace, move, copy or test and pointing at a location with a JSON Pointer.

Sent as the body of an HTTP PATCH it lets a client alter one field without transmitting or overwriting the whole resource. The `test` operation is what makes an update safely conditional: if the document is not in the expected state the patch fails rather than silently clobbering a concurrent edit.

name: application/node
description:
This type labels JavaScript intended to run as a Node.js CommonJS module rather than to be delivered to a browser. The registration is maintained by the Node.js Technical Steering Committee.

The registration is candid about the overlap. It notes that the type "occupies the same file extension as other media types", and that a `.js` file "should be considered ambiguous if the intended execution environment is unknown". Server-side and browser JavaScript share the extension, and a web server should still send [text/javascript](/text/javascript).

name: application/sql
description:
RFC 6922 registers this type so that a file of SQL statements can be labelled as such in transit. The registration deliberately says nothing about which dialect the statements are written in.

That silence matters in practice. A dump from PostgreSQL, from MySQL and from SQLite all carry this same type, and none of them will load into the others unedited. The type tells you the file is SQL, not that your database can read it. The unregistered spelling still in common use is [application/x-sql](/application/x-sql).

name: application/x-sql
description:
This is the unregistered form of the SQL media type, and the one more likely to appear in the wild. It was in use before RFC 6922 registered [application/sql](/application/sql) and carried on afterwards, as `x-` types generally do.

Neither form replaces the other. Tools emit whichever they were written against, and both mean the same thing: a file of SQL statements whose dialect is not stated anywhere in the label.

name: application/zstd
description:
Zstandard is a lossless compression format defined by RFC 8878. At its default setting it reaches roughly gzip's ratio several times faster, and at high settings it compresses considerably harder than gzip can.

Its distinguishing feature is the trained dictionary. Given a sample of the small documents you mean to compress, it derives a dictionary that lets each one compress well despite being far too small for the algorithm to find redundancy in on its own.

furtherReading.title: RFC 8878 - Zstandard Compression and the 'application/zstd' Media Type

name: application/sarif+json
description:
SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) is the OASIS standard for reporting what a code analysis tool found. A run records the tool, the rules it applied, and every result with its location, severity and enough surrounding context to be understood without rerunning the tool.

It exists so that every linter and scanner stops inventing its own output format. GitHub code scanning consumes SARIF, which is most of why analysis tools now emit it alongside whatever they produced before.

name: application/spdx+json
description:
SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange) is the Linux Foundation's standard for describing what a software release contains: its packages, their versions and licences, and the relationships between them. This type is the JSON serialisation of an SPDX document.

It is one of the formats accepted as a software bill of materials, which is what moved SPDX from a licence-compliance tool into something shipped alongside releases and checked by procurement.
